corrections.claimed_speedup: Cold CLI check on home-assistant (no cache, M4): ty 2.19s vs Pyrefly 5.32s vs Pyright 19.62s vs mypy 45.66s, so ty is ~9x faster than Pyright and ~21x faster than mypy (derived from page data). notes: The prose and chart disagree slightly on the LSP numbers (4.7ms/386ms/2.38s vs 4.5ms/370.5ms/2.60s), so both are now in claimed_speedup. tier_reason: The README's 'Comparison with clang-tidy' section says 'significantly faster than clang-tidy (over 10x in my experience)'. This is a first-party number with no benchmark code, codebase, or hardware given, so it is Tier C.

corrections.workload: Running the same clang-tidy checks over a C/C++ codebase (for example in CI). clangd-tidy wraps clangd, which only builds an AST from included headers, instead of standalone clang-tidy, which checks code from all headers even though it suppresses warnings from them by default.
corrections.caveats: 'Over 10x' is the author's personal experience, with no benchmark script, codebase, compiler flags, or hardware given, so it is capped at Tier C despite the plausible-sounding number. The StackOverflow discussion linked in the README is anecdotal, not a reproducible benchmark. The comparison is not exactly like-for-like: clangd-tidy silently disables several clang-tidy checks that clangd does not support, and it lacks --fix.

notes: The quote is verified. The record's claim that clangd 'reuses its background index' is not on the page, so it was removed from workload. Metadata verified: MIT, 161 stars, last commit 2026-02-09 (active). The project is small, but it stays because it is Tier C, not D.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README headline: '10-100x faster than existing linters (like Flake8) and formatters (like Black)'. Founder's blog post (2022-08-30): '~150x faster than Flake8 on macOS (~25x faster if you hack Flake8 to enable multiprocessing)', '~75x faster than pycodestyle', '~50x faster than pyflakes and pylint', and a single-file re-lint of CPython in '~60ms total'. The blog gives no numbers against Black or any formatter.
corrections.workload: Linting the CPython codebase from scratch with no cache, plus incremental single-file re-lint. The formatting speed claim against Black appears only in the README headline, not on the benchmark page.
corrections.caveats: No CPU model is stated for any headline number: the blog says only 'macOS'. The blog post (pre-Astral, by the original creator) is a first-party account with no harness. CONTRIBUTING.md ('CPython Benchmark' section) does give a reproducible head-to-head. It uses hyperfine on the CPython 3.10 branch with ruff built via cargo --release, tool versions from scripts/benchmarks/pyproject.toml, and Python 3.11. Results: Ruff 294ms vs flake8 12.26s (41.66x), pyflakes 15.79s (53.64x), pycodestyle 46.92s (159.43x), autoflake 6.18s (20.98x). It still states no hardware, so the entry stays Tier C. crates/ruff_benchmark contains microbenchmarks of Ruff internals only.

notes: The blog numbers are verified. The record wrongly said no head-to-head harness exists in the repo; CONTRIBUTING.md has one, but it lacks a CPU model, so the tier stays C. The Black claim is README-only. Metadata verified: MIT, 49764 stars, last commit 2026-09-24.

tier_reason: The README benchmark tables compare lld, wild, and mold on 9 programs on a Threadripper 7980X and an M1 Ultra. They state the build configuration (release builds of all linkers as of 2026-08-28, default options, median of 3 after warm-up). The public Zenodo artifact (records/21882261) contains the mold linker, build/evaluation scripts, a container image, and all linker inputs. The artifact belongs to a peer-reviewed ASPLOS 2027 paper.

corrections.caveats: The README numbers are self-reported by the mold maintainer. However, the Zenodo artifact (https://zenodo.org/records/21882261, the ASPLOS 2027 paper artifact, mixed licenses, 27GB bench.tar.gz) includes the build/evaluation scripts, container image, and linker inputs. Hardware, OS, date, and run method are stated. The exact compiler and flags used to build the 9 test programs are not listed in the README. The README tables compare only lld and wild. The companion paper 'mold: A Massively Parallel Linker' (ASPLOS 2027, arXiv 2608.23228) reports '2.4-16.1x faster than ... lld' and 'up to 112x faster than the traditional GNU ld'. mold is now written in Rust (built with Cargo).

notes: Every number in claimed_speedup matches the README tables: 4.9x/1.9x median, 50.73s to 3.15s = 16.1x, 0.56s to 0.25s = 2.3x, and a 1.5x minimum (Clang 21 debug, M1 Ultra). The paper provides a GNU ld comparison that the README lacks. Metadata verified: MIT, 17239 stars, last commit 2026-09-23, primary language Rust.
